reason: The sources provide over 15 multi-site verified facts detailing Charon's discovery, unique orbital mechanics, and physical traits.
story: In June 1978, astronomer James Christy was examining photographic plates of Pluto at the U.S. Naval Observatory when he spotted a strange periodic bulge. That bulge turned out to be Pluto's massive companion world, Charon. Unlike typical moons, Charon possesses about half Pluto's diameter and roughly one-eighth its mass, making it the largest satellite relative to its primary in the Solar System. Because Charon is so exceptionally large, the center of gravity between the two bodies—the barycenter—does not sit inside Pluto at all. Instead, it hovers in empty space roughly 600 miles above Pluto's surface. Pluto and Charon effectively form a double world, locked in an eternal gravitational embrace where each always shows the exact same face to the other as they orbit their shared empty fulcrum every 6.4 Earth days. Christy named the moon after his wife, Charlene, cleverly matching the underworld ferryman of myth.
angle: Charon is so massive compared to Pluto that Pluto does not orbit its own center—both worlds orbit a shared empty point in space between them.

claims.claim: Charon was discovered by astronomer James Christy.
Charon was discovered by noticing a recurring elongation or bulge on photographic plates of Pluto.
The periodic bulge matched Pluto's known rotational period of approximately 6.4 days.
Charon is the largest of Pluto's five known moons.
Charon has roughly half the diameter of Pluto.
Charon has approximately one-eighth of Pluto's mass.
The center of mass (barycenter) of the Pluto–Charon system lies in empty space outside of Pluto.
Pluto and Charon are mutually tidally locked, meaning each always presents the same face to the other.
Pluto and Charon orbit each other once every 6.4 Earth days.
The Pluto–Charon system is often referred to or considered as a binary or double dwarf planet system.
The average distance separating Pluto and Charon is approximately 19,600 kilometers (around 12,200 miles).
Charon was named by James Christy partly in honor of his wife Charlene, whose nickname was Char.
The name Charon also represents the mythological ferryman of the dead associated with Pluto.
Charon displays a distinct reddish north polar region.
NASA's New Horizons spacecraft made its flyby of the Pluto–Charon system in July 2015.
Unlike Pluto, Charon has no significant or bound atmosphere.

disputed: Co-discovery credit: S3 lists Robert Harrington alongside James Christy for the discovery, whereas S1 and S2 attribute the discovery solely to Christy. Scripts should attribute the primary discovery to Christy while mentioning Harrington as a collaborating astronomer according to NASA.

Name pronunciation: S1 and S7 describe debate over whether to use the classical hard /k/ or Christy's preferred soft /ʃ/ based on his wife's name. Scripts can highlight this as a quirky linguistic disagreement between classical scholars and NASA mission scientists.
